references.text: Sarai says that the Lord has prevented her from having children and asks Abram to go in to Hagar. This shows the same theme of human frustration over barrenness and God's role in fertility.
The Lord had closed every womb in Abimelech's house because of Sarah, demonstrating God's direct control over fertility—the same point Jacob makes to Rachel.
The Lord saw that Leah was unloved and opened her womb, while Rachel remained barren. This is the direct background for Rachel's frustration and Jacob's response.
God remembered Rachel and opened her womb, confirming Jacob's statement that it is God, not he, who controls fertility.
Joseph says to his brothers, 'Am I in the place of God?'—a direct verbal parallel to Jacob's words in 30:2, expressing human limitation before God's sovereignty.
The Lord had closed Hannah's womb. A closely parallel example of God's sovereignty over fertility and a woman's pain over barrenness.
The Naaman story: The king of Israel says, 'Am I God, who can kill and make alive?'—a parallel to Jacob's rejection of having divine power over life and fertility.
Both verses reveal Jacob's human weakness and anger in conflicted relationships, adding depth to his character throughout the narrative.
